newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. forces in Kuwait fire big guns near Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. forces in Kuwait fire big guns near Iraq.

text.p: Hundreds of heavily armed U.S. soldier fired artillery and tank cannon in the Kuwaiti desert on Sunday in wargames aimed at deterring trouble from former occupier Iraq, a U.S. military official said.

The troops carried out the live-fire exercise at the Kuwaiti military's Adera Range desert training area 40 km (25 miles) south of the Iraqi border, Lieutenant-Colonel Thomas Nickerson said by telephone.

Kuwaitis said the training was taking place in unusually unpleasant, dusty conditions in the desert. The sky over Kuwait City was darkened by a thick cloud of sand and dust stirred by a dust storm overnight in the desert interior.
Nickerson said a fresh batch of 200 U.S. troops arrived in Kuwait on Saturday night from Fort Hood, Texas, and were preparing to move into the desert with heavy weaponry.
Their arrival brought to about 1,500 the number of U.S. Cavalry 1st Division soldiers so far sent to Kuwait in the latest flare-up with Baghdad.
In all 3,000 troops were ordered to Kuwait at short notice as part of efforts to deter any possible Iraqi military moves against its neighbours.

The troops are joining about 1,200 soldiers already in Kuwait before the latest Gulf crisis began. The ground troops' formal mission is to train Kuwaiti forces, but officials said they could be used in any military action against Iraq.

Strengthening another arm of the U.S. buildup in the Gulf, a second U.S. aircraft carrier, the USS Enterprise, began sending warplanes on Sunday to patrol a Western-imposed no-fly zone in southern Iraq.

"In terms of national resolve the presence of a carrier is a very definite message that is very hard to misinterpret," Rear-Admiral Martin J. Mayer, Commander of the USS Enterprise battle group, told reporters on the carrier's steel runway.
Fresh tension arose between Washington and Baghdad in late August when Baghdad's forces intervened to help a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq.

Washington retaliated by firing 44 cruise missiles at air defence targets in southern Iraq on September 3 and 4. It also expanded the southern no-fly zone by pushing its northern limit up to the 33rd parallel from the 32nd parallel.

The Enterprise, carrying 74 aircraft including F-14 fighters recently modified to deliver laser-guided bombs, entered the Gulf on Thursday to join another carrier battle group plus U.S. ground and air forces deployed mainly in Kuwait against Iraq.

The United States, Britain and France imposed no-fly zones in Iraq in 1992 to protect southern Iraqi Shi'ites and northern Iraqi Kurds who rebelled against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein after the 1991 conflict ended Iraq's ocupation of Kuwait.
